title: Futures, Promises, Async and Thread Pools
objectives: Carry a value or an exception from one thread to another with std::promise/std::future, and explain why future::get() consumes the state
Wrap callables with std::packaged_task and choose std::async launch policies deliberately (async vs deferred)
Explain the std::async destructor gotcha and why the default launch policy is a portability trap
Design a minimal thread pool: task queue + condition variable + packaged_task-backed submit() returning futures
motivation: Threads give you parallelism, but returning a result by hand, shared slots, flags, condition variables, is plumbing you will get wrong under deadline pressure. Futures are the standard plumbing: a one-shot channel that carries a value or an exception from producer to consumer, with blocking get() as the rendezvous. Pricing a book of a thousand instruments across cores is exactly this pattern at scale, and a thread pool is how you stop paying thread-creation costs on every tick while bounding parallelism.

blocks.text: promise and future: a one-shot channel

blocks.md: A `std::promise<T>` is the write end of a single-use channel; `future<T>` (from `get_future()`) is the read end. The producer calls `set_value()` (or `set_exception()`); the consumer calls `get()`, which **blocks until the value or exception arrives**, then returns the value, or rethrows the exception, in the consumer's thread. `get()` **consumes** the future: call it twice and you get `std::future_error`. This channel is *one-shot*; for repeated communication use the queues of the previous lesson.

blocks.caption: The promise is moved into the worker; the future stays with main. get() is the synchronisation point, the output is deterministic: 42.

blocks.md: The channel also transports **exceptions**: if the worker throws before `set_value()`, the exception object is stored in the shared state and `get()` rethrows it in the consuming thread, so failure travels the same pipe as success, and the consumer decides the policy. If you need many readers of one result, call `fut.share()` to get a `std::shared_future`, which can be `get()`-ed by every holder. And keep the direction honest: a future is not a queue, it is a single rendezvous, reusable channels back to the mutex-and-condition-variable tools of the previous lesson.

`std::packaged_task<R(Args...)>` wraps any callable and, when invoked, stores the result (or the thrown exception) into a future from `get_future()`. It is the bridge between "a function I want to run" and "a value I want to await", which is why thread pools are built on it. `std::async` is the convenience wrapper: give it a callable and it manages the thread and the future for you. What it does *not* do is promise a thread, that depends on the launch policy.

rows: True parallelism; future's destructor blocks until done
Nowhere yet, runs on get()/wait(), in the calling thread
Implementation chooses async or deferred per call
Portability trap: "parallel" code may silently run serially

blocks.title: The std::async destructor gotcha
blocks.md: The future returned by `std::async` with `launch::async` **waits for the task to finish in its destructor**, unique among futures. A temporary future (e.g. `std::async(std::launch::async, work);` as a statement) therefore runs synchronously. Meanwhile the default policy may pick `deferred`, so "async" code can run on one thread at a time. Production rule: pass an explicit `std::launch::async` and keep the future alive until you need the result.

blocks.caption: Fan-out: two legs priced concurrently, joined at get(). Deterministic output because futures carry values, not shared mutable state.

blocks.md: Why pool at all? Creating and destroying a thread costs tens of microseconds plus scheduler churn; market-data tasks are often shorter than that. A pool also **bounds parallelism**, 8 workers on 8 cores, not 200 threads fighting the cache. The design is the previous lesson's primitives assembled once: N worker threads, a shared task queue guarded by a mutex, a condition variable, and a `submit()` that wraps your callable in a `packaged_task` and hands back its future.

blocks.caption: Every piece is from lessons 1-2: RAII threads, a mutex protecting the queue, a while-pattern wait (via wait(lk, pred)), and packaged_task for the result channel. Note the task runs outside the lock.

blocks.md: Futures are promises with a receipt: `std::future<T>` is the handle for a value that does not exist yet, `std::promise`/`std::packaged_task` is the writing end, and the thread pool is the machinery deciding when the promise gets fulfilled. Their whole point is to decouple *expressing* parallelism ("these three computations are independent") from *managing* it (thread lifetimes, join points, exception transport), the management being exactly the part everyone gets wrong when they write raw `std::thread` code.

blocks.caption: Three independent sums, two helper threads, one join, exceptions travel through .get().

blocks.md: The details that futures quietly get right, and that hand-rolled threading gets wrong: **exception transport**, an exception in the worker is captured and rethrown at `.get()`, so errors are not silently swallowed; **join-on-destruction**, a `std::future` from `std::async` blocks in its destructor, eliminating the "forgot to join" class of bugs; and **one-shot semantics**, `get()` invalidates the future, which matches how results are actually consumed and prevents accidental double-reads. The remaining footgun is the launch policy: `std::launch::deferred` (the fallback when you do not specify) runs the work lazily *on the calling thread at get()*, parallelism that silently never happened. Say `std::launch::async` out loud or do not expect concurrency.

blocks.title: Thread pools, tasks and the futures they break
blocks.md: A real pool (or `std::async` on a loaded runtime) executes tasks on threads you do not own, which breaks code that assumes the executing thread (thread-local caches, affinity-pinned hot paths, lock hierarchies by thread id). Additionally, futures are one-shot and their `get()` blocks; when you need composable pipelines (continue-when-ready, not wait-until-done), you leave std::future for continuation-style libraries ( folly::Future, std::experimental ) or coroutines, the design lesson being: the standard future is a fine receipt and a poor dataflow engine.

blocks.title: Fan-out pricing on the pool
blocks.md: Per tick: submit one task per instrument, collect `future<Price>` objects, then `get()` them and combine. Results are deterministic regardless of scheduling because each result travels through its own future, no shared mutable state. The pool bounds the parallelism to core count, keeping tail latencies stable; a real pool adds priorities so a hedge-recalc task cannot queue behind a report.

guidedExercise.prompt: Using the ThreadPool above, write a `fanout_pnl(const std::vector<double>& legs)` that submits one task per leg, collects all futures, and returns the sum of the legs' absolute contributions after they complete. Legs are `+120.50, -80.25, +15.75, -5.00`. Then answer: (a) why is it safe to `get()` the futures in any order, and (b) why must you keep every future alive rather than calling `pool.submit(...)` as a bare statement?
hints: Each submit returns its own future<R>; store them in a vector before submitting the next.
futures are independent channels, get() on one does not touch another.
A discarded future from submit() is harmless, but discipline matters when you switch to std::async, whose future blocks in its destructor.

independentExercise.prompt: You must price 12 independent legs, each taking 10 ms of pure CPU, on a machine with 4 cores. (1) Using a 4-worker thread pool, compute the best-case makespan. (2) Compare with launching 12 `std::thread`s and with `std::async(std::launch::deferred, ...)` on all 12. (3) A colleague writes `auto f = std::async(price_leg, 1);` with no explicit policy and calls it 'parallel'. What is wrong with the claim, and what is the one-character-class fix?
hints: With 4 workers, tasks run in waves of 4, count the waves.
deferred means the work happens at get(), one at a time, in the calling thread.
The default launch policy lets the implementation choose deferred, so 'parallel' is an implementation detail, not a guarantee.
independentExercise.solution: **(1) Pool of 4:** 12 tasks / 4 workers = 3 full waves x 10 ms = **30 ms** best case (assuming perfect balance and no overhead). **(2) 12 threads:** also ~30 ms of compute if 4 run concurrently and the OS schedules the rest, but you pay ~12 thread creations and oversubscribe the cores, which adds jitter. **Deferred:** all 12 run at `get()` time in one thread: 12 x 10 ms = **120 ms**, zero parallelism. **(3)** The claim is not guaranteed: the default policy permits the implementation to run the task deferred, i.e. serially at get(). The fix is to write `std::async(std::launch::async, price_leg, 1)` - an explicit policy turns 'maybe parallel' into 'parallel', and you should also keep `f` alive until you call `get()` because an async-policy future blocks in its destructor.

commonMistakes: Calling future::get() twice, the first call consumes the shared state; the second throws std::future_error.
Using the default std::async policy and assuming parallelism, it may choose deferred, running tasks serially at get().
Discarding the future from std::async(std::launch::async, ...): it blocks in its destructor, turning your 'async' call into a synchronous one.
Running the dequeued task while still holding the pool's queue mutex, serialises all workers and kills the pool's throughput.
Queueing a move-only callable directly into std::function<void()>, packaged_task is move-only, hence the shared_ptr wrapper in submit().
realWorldApplication: Thread pools with future-returning submit() are the standard execution layer of servers, backtesters and market-data pipelines; every job system from database engines to build tools uses exactly the queue + workers + packaged-task shape shown here.
quantFinanceApplication: Tick-time pricing fans out one task per instrument and folds the futures into a portfolio number; the pool bounds parallelism so a burst of ticks cannot spawn hundreds of threads. The exercise's 12-legs-on-4-cores arithmetic is the desk's core-count budgeting question.
summary: promise/future is a one-shot channel carrying a value or an exception; get() blocks, delivers, and consumes the state.
packaged_task turns any callable into a future-producing job, the glue thread pools are built on.
std::async needs an explicit std::launch::async for guaranteed parallelism; deferred runs at get() in the calling thread, and the default policy may silently pick it.
The future returned by async (async policy) waits for task completion in its destructor, a unique, easy-to-miss behaviour.
A minimal pool = worker threads + mutex-guarded task queue + condition variable + packaged_task-backed submit(); run tasks outside the lock.

quiz.prompt: With std::async(std::launch::deferred, f), when does f actually execute?
options: On a new thread, immediately when async is called
When get() or wait() is called, in the calling thread
It never executes unless get() throws
quiz.explanation: Deferred tasks are lazy: they run lazily at get()/wait() in the thread that calls it, useful for lazy evaluation, useless for parallelism.
The first get() returns 10 (so 10+5=15) and consumes the shared state. The second get() on the now-invalid future throws std::future_error, which the catch prints as "gone".

quiz.prompt: What is unusual about the future returned by std::async with the async policy?
options: It can be copied to share the result
Its destructor waits for the task to finish
It throws if the task has not started
quiz.explanation: Unique among futures, an async-policy future's destructor blocks until the task completes, which is why discarding it (e.g. as a temporary) silently serialises your code.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about std::packaged_task are true?
options: It wraps a callable and stores the invocation's result into a future
get_future() can be called only once per task
The result (or exception) is stored when the task is invoked, not when it is created
It is copyable, so it can be stored directly in std::function
quiz.explanation: packaged_task is move-only (option 4 is false), which is exactly why the pool's submit() wraps it in a shared_ptr before putting it in a std::function queue.

quiz.prompt: A 4-worker thread pool processes 12 independent 10 ms CPU-bound tasks. What is the best-case makespan in milliseconds (ignore overheads)?
quiz.explanation: 12 tasks in waves of 4 = 3 waves x 10 ms = 30 ms. With more tasks than workers, makespan is ceil(tasks/workers) x task time, the reason pool sizing is a latency decision.

quiz.prompt: Give two concrete reasons a server uses a fixed thread pool instead of creating a thread per task.
quiz.modelAnswer: Thread creation and destruction cost tens of microseconds, which dwarfs short tasks and adds tail latency; a fixed pool also bounds parallelism to the core count, avoiding oversubscription, cache thrashing and scheduler jitter.
quiz.explanation: The two levers are per-task setup cost (latency) and controlling concurrency (stability). Pools trade a little queueing for predictable tail behaviour, the same argument as connection pooling.

flashcards.back: Blocks until the shared state is ready, returns the value (or rethrows the stored exception) in the caller, and CONSUMES the state, a second get() throws std::future_error.

async: run on a new thread now; its future blocks in its destructor. deferred: run at get()/wait() in the calling thread, lazy, never parallel. Default policy: implementation may pick either per call.

flashcards.front: Role of packaged_task in a thread pool
flashcards.back: It wraps the user's callable, exposes get_future(), and stores the result/exception when invoked, the mechanism that lets submit() return a future.

flashcards.front: promise set_value(10); cout << f.get() + 5; then a second f.get(): what happens?
flashcards.back: Prints 15; the second get() throws std::future_error because get() consumed the shared state.
